title: Trump Just Gutted the Only Federal Agency Devoted to Election Security. Four Months Before the Midterms.
excerpt: The president fired the last two members of the Election Assistance Commission on Thursday, leaving the body unable to certify voting systems, distribute security funds, or maintain the national voter registration form — as the administration simultaneously pushes states to purge voter rolls of naturalized citizens.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The Election Assistance Commission is now inoperative after Trump fired its last two members.
  • The commission's paralysis jeopardizes election security and support for states ahead of the midterms.
  • Federal assistance for election preparation has significantly declined due to the commission's lack of leadership.
  • Naturalized citizens face increased risks of being purged from voter rolls amid new administration directives.
  • Senator Warner warns that these actions raise serious concerns about political interference in election oversight.
Election Assistance Commission in Crisis
›EAC has zero commissioners after recent firings.
›Commission needs at least three members to function.
›Federal election security funding to states has dropped significantly.
›States report no timely threat briefings from federal agencies.

The Election Assistance Commission no longer has a single commissioner. As of Thursday evening, the only federal agency in the United States devoted solely to helping states run elections has been rendered inoperative — four months before voters go to the polls in November's midterm elections.

President Trump terminated the commission's last two members, Chairman Thomas Hicks and Commissioner Benjamin Hovland, both of whom had been unanimously confirmed by the Senate. A third commissioner, Republican Christy McCormick, resigned on June 9. A fourth seat has been vacant since earlier this year.

The agency needs at least three commissioners to approve any action. It now has zero.

"These removals leave the agency without leadership and unable to carry out its major responsibilities," said Michael Waldman, president of the Brennan Center for Justice at New York University.

What the commission does — and can no longer do

The EAC was created by Congress in 2002 after the hanging-chad debacle of the 2000 presidential election. It certifies and tests voting systems, distributes federal election security funding to states, and maintains the national mail voter registration form — the standard template used by millions of Americans.

> ""These removals leave the agency without leadership and unable to carry out its major responsibilities," said Michael Waldman, president of the Brennan Center for Justice at New York University."

Without commissioners, none of that work can move forward. States preparing for the November midterms have already reported a significant drop in federal assistance, and officials say they no longer expect to receive timely threat briefings from other federal agencies either.

Earlier this year, the commission approved extra security funding for election officials. During the pandemic, it worked with states to make mail balloting broadly accessible. That institutional knowledge is now frozen in place.

A broader campaign against election oversight

The firings do not exist in isolation. They come days after the Justice Department sent letters to all 50 states warning that election officials could face criminal prosecution for allowing naturalized citizens to remain on voter rolls — a move widely interpreted as targeting immigrants who have become U.S. citizens.

In a separate development, a federal judge this week blocked the Trump administration from using an expanded version of the SAVE database — originally designed to verify immigration status for public benefits — as a mass voter-citizenship checker. The ruling found the administration had violated federal privacy protections.

And FEMA has begun withholding 20 per cent of terrorism prevention grants from states unless they comply with the administration's election directives, including using the SAVE database to verify the citizenship of every person on their voter rolls within 120 days.

Why naturalized Indian Americans should pay attention

More than 2.7 million Indian Americans are estimated to be U.S. citizens, many of them naturalized. Voter-roll purge systems that cross-reference immigration databases are known to produce false positives — flagging naturalized citizens as non-citizens because government records have not been updated to reflect their change in status.

Impact on Naturalized Citizens
›Over 2.7 million Indian Americans are U.S. citizens, many naturalized.
›Voter-roll purges may incorrectly flag naturalized citizens as non-citizens.
›Outdated databases increase risks of wrongful voter removal.
›Federal election infrastructure is less capable of ensuring fair elections.

The Brennan Center and the League of Women Voters have warned that the SAVE database is frequently outdated, meaning immigrants who have been lawfully naturalized can be wrongly flagged and removed from voter rolls — sometimes without notice.

Combined with the EAC's paralysis, the effect is a federal election infrastructure that is simultaneously less capable of supporting fair elections and more aggressive about challenging the eligibility of naturalized voters.

Senator Mark Warner of Virginia, a Democrat, said the firings "should concern every American, regardless of party."

"Removing every remaining commissioner just months before the 2026 midterm elections is an extraordinary step that demands an immediate explanation from the administration and raises profound concerns about political interference in the institutions that support our elections," Warner said.

What comes next

The White House issued a statement saying the president "reserves the right to remove individuals that may not be totally aligned with the important task of securing America's elections." A White House official cited a June 29 Supreme Court decision granting Trump broad power over the leadership of independent agencies.

By law, the president can appoint replacements, but nominees must be split evenly between Democrats and Republicans and confirmed by the Senate. That process could take months — pushing well past the November midterms.

For the roughly 1.4 million Indian Americans registered to vote across the country, the message is urgent: verify your registration, keep documentation of your citizenship status readily accessible, and watch for any notices from state election offices. The systems designed to protect your right to vote are being tested in real time.
image_caption: The U.S. Election Assistance Commission, now without any commissioners for the first time in its history
nri_angle: The gutting of the EAC comes alongside voter-roll purge systems that disproportionately flag naturalized citizens — including the 2.7 million Indian Americans who are U.S. citizens — as ineligible to vote.
author: Diaspora Desk
